channel.title: Same Day, Years Apart | anoni.net News
channel.description: One event a day from the history of privacy, anonymity networks and censorship, with a new look back added on the same date every year.

item.title: Account data email providers hand over to governments
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Data from your email account may be disclosed in response to lawful government requests (Yahoo's privacy policy for Taiwan, read in November 2026, is one example). On this day, Yahoo announced a settlement with the families of a journalist and a dissident jailed in China, in a lawsuit over account data it gave the authorities, with no amount made public at the time.
item.content:encoded: Yahoo's terms for Taiwan name a company with a Taipei address as the provider of Yahoo Mail and apply Republic of China law, yet its privacy policy there says information may be processed and stored outside your country of residence and disclosed in response to lawful government requests, without naming the countries or governments involved (both read on 8 November 2026). On 13 November 2007, Yahoo announced that it had settled a US lawsuit brought by the families of two people jailed in China, a journalist and a dissident, with the terms kept confidential and no amount made public at the time (Yahoo announced in 2021 that its services would no longer be accessible from mainland China from 1 November, according to a Reuters report carried by the Business & Human Rights Resource Centre). The families argued that the data Yahoo gave Chinese authorities directly led to the two arrests and convictions, according to MIT Technology Review, while Yahoo argued that Chinese law required it to hand over the data and its lawyers said it was unclear what role, if any, the data had played. A US House Foreign Affairs Committee press release lists the account data Chinese authorities requested on the journalist as the IP address (a network number that can be used to trace where a connection came from), login history and several weeks of email content, and gives the journalist's sentence as 10 years for divulging state secrets. Wherever you live, you can open your own provider's terms of service and privacy policy to check which company provides your mailbox and which law applies (our suggestion).

item.title: Online checks before your Mac opens an app
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: When your Mac opens an app downloaded from the internet, it connects to Apple to check the app for known malware. On this day, a problem with Apple's notarization service left Macs around the world stuck for minutes or unable to open third-party apps at all.
item.content:encoded: When your Mac opens an app downloaded from the internet, macOS's Gatekeeper feature connects to Apple to check whether the app contains known malware and whether the developer's certificate has been revoked, and Apple's support page, checked on 8 November 2026, says the malware check (notarization) runs over an encrypted connection and that your IP address is not logged during certificate checks. Engadget reported that Apple confirmed on its system status page for developers a problem with the notarization service on the afternoon of 12 November 2020, US Eastern time, and that in the same window Macs could hang for minutes or fail to open third-party apps, whether or not they had been updated to the new macOS Big Sur. A security researcher argued in a blog post that day, and in later additions, that macOS sent Apple an identifier for every program it ran, unencrypted and together with the user's IP address, while Apple's support page, updated on 16 November, stated that data from these checks had never been combined with information about users or their devices. The same page said Apple had stopped logging IP addresses for developer certificate checks and promised improvements within a year, including an encrypted protocol for certificate revocation checks and a setting that lets users opt out of the checks; the current page no longer carries that promise or any sentence on those two changes. In System Settings, under Privacy & Security, the Security section is where you choose which sources your Mac can open apps from (the App Store only, or also identified developers); the current support page describes no setting for turning the online checks off, and neither do its Taiwan and mainland China versions, both published on 1 June 2026 with the same privacy section.

item.title: Anti-cheat and copy protection software running at the lowest layer of Windows
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Some games on your computer come with anti-cheat software that runs at the lowest layer of Windows (checked in November 2026). On this day, Sony BMG suspended the manufacture of CDs containing XCP, copy protection software that hid its own files on computers.
item.content:encoded: Some games on your computer come with anti-cheat software that runs a driver in the Windows kernel, the lowest layer of the operating system; Riot Games' support page, checked on 8 November 2026, lists one as part of Vanguard and links to removal steps. A researcher reported on a blog in late October 2005 that XCP, the copy protection software on Sony BMG music CDs, hid files and running programs whose names began with a set prefix and had no entry in the Control Panel's Add or Remove Programs list. Sony BMG suspended the manufacture of XCP CDs as a precaution on 11 November 2005, according to a company statement quoted by Betanews, and on 18 November Sony Music Japan International announced it had asked dealers in Japan to stop selling 40 imported XCP titles and pull shop stock, PC Watch reported. In January 2007, the US Federal Trade Commission published a proposed settlement barring Sony BMG from installing copy protection software that consumers could not readily find or remove. On Windows, you can turn on memory integrity, which makes it harder for malicious programs to use drivers to take over your PC, under Device security > Core isolation details in the Windows Security app; if Windows reports an incompatible driver, Microsoft suggests asking the device manufacturer for an updated one.

item.title: Signal blocked at your Myanmar contacts' end
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Signal on your friends' phones in Myanmar was blocked by the authorities in 2024, according to Freedom House. On this day, a special court inside a Myanmar prison sentenced a blogger to 20 years and six months after a closed trial.
item.content:encoded: If you message friends or colleagues in Myanmar on Signal, Freedom House's 2025 report says authorities there blocked Signal and major VPNs (services that route your connection through another server, often to get around blocking) in June and July 2024, before the military adopted a Cybersecurity Law in January 2025. Under an unofficial English translation, the law requires ministry permission to set up or provide a VPN; RFA reported it as penalising unauthorised provision, while Access Now said it also criminalises use. According to the press freedom group RSF, a blogger who ran internet cafés in Yangon was arrested with a video banned by the military government, and on 10 November 2008 a special court inside Yangon's Insein Prison sentenced him to 20 years and six months. CPJ, another press freedom group, recorded that the trial was held behind closed doors and that 15 years of the sentence came under the "Electronic Act", and he was freed in an amnesty in January 2012. In website connection tests run in Myanmar by the censorship measurement project OONI from July to September 2026, about 27,000 to 39,000 results a month were flagged as anomalous (an anomaly is not a confirmed block), and you can look up local connectivity on OONI Explorer.

item.title: Firefox's default tracking protection
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Firefox on your desktop has by default let a cookie be used only on the site that created it since June 2022, and Firefox's development source code was still set that way when checked in November 2026. On this day, the Mozilla Foundation released Firefox 1.0 with a built-in pop-up blocker and features to help guard against phishing sites.
item.content:encoded: Firefox on your desktop by default lets a cookie (a small file a website stores in your browser) be used only on the site that created it. Mozilla's June 2022 announcement said this default applies to all Firefox desktop users worldwide and stops tracking companies from following your browsing across sites, and it was still set that way in Firefox's development source code when we checked on 8 November 2026. On 9 November 2004, the Mozilla Foundation released Firefox 1.0, available in Japanese the same day according to Japan's Internet Watch, and its press release listed a built-in pop-up blocker and a clear display of secure sites' real identity to help guard against phishing and spoofed sites. In mainland China, the Chinese news site IT之家 and CyberInsider reported in July 2025 that Beijing Firefox (北京谋智火狐信息技术有限公司), Firefox's local operator, would end its account, sync and community services later that year, though the browser could still be downloaded from firefox.com. If you use Firefox and have not changed the cookie setting, you do not need to turn anything on, and on other browsers you can look for an option to block tracking cookies.

item.title: When a business in Japan sends your personal data abroad
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Your personal data generally needs your prior consent before a business in Japan sends it abroad, under Japanese law as checked in November 2026. On this day, the Council of Europe opened for signature a protocol requiring Parties to set up fully independent data protection authorities and to restrict transfers of personal data to non-Parties unless they ensure adequate protection.
item.content:encoded: If a business in Japan hands your personal data to a third party abroad, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (Act No. 57 of 2003, checked on e-Gov on 7 November 2026) generally requires your prior consent to the transfer abroad. The consent requirement does not apply when the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) has designated the country in its rules as having protection equivalent to Japan's, or when the recipient has a system that meets the PPC's standards, though in that second case the business must take the measures needed to ensure the recipient keeps up equivalent measures. On 8 November 2001, the Council of Europe (a separate organisation from the European Union) opened for signature an Additional Protocol to the Convention for the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data, requiring each Party to set up supervisory authorities that act in complete independence and hear claims from any person about the processing of personal data. The Protocol also allows transfers to a recipient in a state or organisation that is not a Party to the Convention only if it ensures an adequate level of protection, with two exceptions: domestic law permits the transfer for specific interests of the data subject or legitimate prevailing interests, especially important public interests, or the controller sending the data provides safeguards, such as contractual clauses, that the competent authorities find adequate. Article 133 of the Act provides that the PPC's chairperson and members exercise their authority independently, and when a business in Japan asks for your consent to a transfer abroad, the Act requires it to tell you first about that country's personal data protection system, the measures the recipient takes and other relevant information.

item.title: Storage locations for WeChat users' personal data
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: If you signed up for WeChat with a phone number outside mainland China's +86 dialling code, your personal information is stored on servers in Singapore and Malaysia under WeChat's privacy policy, or in Hong Kong for users in Hong Kong and Macao. On this day, the Standing Committee of China's National People's Congress passed the Cybersecurity Law, requiring operators of critical information infrastructure to store personal information collected in China inside the country in principle.
item.content:encoded: If you use WeChat outside mainland China with a phone number that does not carry the +86 dialling code, then under WeChat's privacy policy (updated on 6 August 2026, checked on 3 November) your personal information is stored on servers in Singapore and Malaysia, or in Hong Kong for users in Hong Kong and Macao, with WeChat International as the data controller for users outside the EEA, the UK, Switzerland and mainland China. Under the same policy, your data may in limited cases be accessed remotely from mainland China for technical support, and information from your interactions with Weixin users (Tencent classes accounts registered with +86 numbers as Weixin) is shared with Weixin, which processes it in mainland China to the extent necessary. On 7 November 2016, the Standing Committee of China's National People's Congress passed the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China, which requires operators of critical information infrastructure (systems in key sectors such as communications, energy and finance, with the scope set separately by the State Council) to store personal information and important data collected and generated in China inside the country, subject to a security assessment where a transfer abroad is genuinely necessary; the amendment in force since 1 January 2026 left this requirement unchanged. In its Weixin privacy guidelines for +86 accounts, in effect since 17 August, Tencent writes that personal information collected in China is in principle stored in China as laws and regulations require, without naming which ones, while the WeChat privacy policy contains no explanation of how its storage arrangements relate to Chinese law. To see what WeChat holds about you, go to "Me" > "Settings" > "My Information & Authorizations" and select "Export Personal Data" (the policy lists only the English menu names), and the export covers categories including account data, contacts, Moments, favourites, and location and login data.

item.title: The email address and phone number tied to your account
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The email address or phone number you give X when signing up is linked to your account under the privacy policy in effect since January. On this day, US prosecutors made public a criminal complaint accusing two former Twitter employees of looking up data on critics of the Saudi government on that government's behalf.
item.content:encoded: Under X's privacy policy in effect since 15 January 2026, creating an account on X (formerly Twitter) requires either an email address or a phone number, and whichever you give is associated with your account. On 6 November 2019, the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California made public a criminal complaint (an allegation not yet tested at trial) charging two former Twitter employees and a Saudi national with acting as illegal agents of the Saudi government. According to the Justice Department's press release, the two employees used their employee credentials without authorisation to look up information on users critical of the Saudi government, including email addresses, phone numbers, IP addresses and dates of birth that could have been used to identify and locate the people behind the posts. Later Justice Department press releases and the Supreme Court's ruling show that a jury convicted one of the former employees in 2022 and he was sentenced to 42 months in prison, and that in June 2026 the Supreme Court reversed and remanded the appeals court's judgment on a single count, falsifying records, over where that charge could be tried. Carriers in Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea and Japan must confirm a subscriber's identity when issuing a mobile number (in Singapore, a licence condition for prepaid cards), so we infer that a phone number on an X account may lead back to the person it is registered to.

item.title: What Android phones with Google apps send to Google
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Your Android phone with Google apps preinstalled may regularly send Google details such as crash reports and the apps you have installed, as Google's privacy policy still said when we checked on 2 November. On this day, Google and 33 other companies formed an alliance and announced Android, an open-source platform for mobile phones.
item.content:encoded: If your Android phone was sold by Google or one of its partners and comes with Google Play Services and apps such as Gmail and Maps, Google's privacy policy says it periodically contacts Google's servers to provide information including your device type, carrier name, crash reports, the apps you have installed and, depending on your device settings, other information about how you use the device. According to the press release from the time, 34 companies, among them Google and Taiwan's HTC, formed the Open Handset Alliance on 5 November 2007 and announced that they would release Android, a platform for mobile devices, under an open-source licence. Android's official overview now says the operating system's source code is available for anyone to use, while Google's apps and services form a separate set that only Android-compatible devices can be licensed to preinstall. In mainland China, GreatFire's third-party tests found the website play.google.com 100% blocked as of 1 November, and the Google documents we read do not say whether phones sold there come with Google's apps. If you would rather not send Google details such as your battery level and how often you use your apps, open Settings → Google → More → Usage & diagnostics and turn it off, though the menu may sit elsewhere on some brands (Google's account help page said as of 2 November that this still lets the phone get Android updates and does not affect what apps collect, without saying whether the items listed in the privacy policy stop as well).

item.title: Collection of overseas communications with help from US service providers
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: If you live outside the US and use American email or cloud services, the companies running them may be directed by the US government to help collect communications of non-US persons abroad. On this day, the US government formally announced the creation of the National Security Agency, responsible for communications intelligence.
item.content:encoded: Section 702 of the US Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) lets the Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence, in order to acquire foreign intelligence information, target persons reasonably believed to be located outside the United States who are not US persons, and direct an email, cloud or messaging provider in writing to help with the collection, so a non-US person in Asia who uses American services can be a target of such collection. The US president set up the National Security Agency (NSA) for the government's communications intelligence by a memorandum dated 24 October 1952 and held the formal announcement until Election Day, 4 November (per the NSA's page and FAS's Secrecy News citing the NSA, neither of which describes its role in Section 702 collection). A note in the US Code states that Section 702 was repealed effective 12 June 2026 except for transition procedures, and while we found no extension bill when we checked on 2 November, the Brennan Center, an advocacy group, wrote in June that collection would continue until March 2027. Apple's transparency report counts FISA court orders without saying which relate to Section 702, and to list content and non-content data (subscriber, transaction and connection data) separately the law requires it to report six months late in bands of 500, so we infer that you cannot tell from it whether your account is included. For readers in Taiwan, Article 7 of the Communication Security and Surveillance Act is a different rule that covers the communications of foreign forces, of hostile forces outside the territory, or of their personnel, rather than those of ordinary users, and it does not mention service providers (we summarize only its main conditions); for Section 702, none of the sources describe anything users can do to avoid collection.

item.title: Browser signals asking websites not to sell or share your data
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Some browsers can send websites a signal on your behalf asking them not to sell or share your personal data. On this day, California voters passed a privacy law by ballot measure, giving residents the right to stop businesses from sharing their personal information.
item.content:encoded: Some browsers can attach a Global Privacy Control (GPC) signal when you connect to a website, and the GPC website says the signal is meant to communicate a request not to sell or share your personal data under the California Consumer Privacy Act. According to the California Secretary of State's results and voter guide, on 3 November 2020 California voters approved Proposition 24, the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 (CPRA), with 56.2% of the vote, and the act gave the power to set technical specifications for such signals to a newly created California Privacy Protection Agency. The agency's current regulations require businesses that sell or share personal information to treat a signal meeting those specifications as a valid opt-out request, but the act defines a consumer as a California resident, so we infer that readers living elsewhere, Asia included, gain no protection under this law by turning GPC on. Japan regulates a different step: under its Telecommunications Business Act, as amended with effect from 16 June 2023, online services such as messaging, social media, search and news that use tags to send user data to outside parties must notify users or publish what is sent, or else obtain consent or offer a way to stop it, and the ministry's explainer we read does not mention browser signals such as GPC (checked 23 October 2026). Anyone who wants to send the signal can use the DuckDuckGo browser or install DuckDuckGo's extension in their current browser (its help page said as of 2 November that both have GPC on by default), though none of the sources say whether websites honour signals from users outside California.

item.title: System updates left uninstalled
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: If your phone has not installed its security updates, others may be able to exploit flaws in its software over the internet. On this day, a program began spreading across the internet, using software flaws to break into one computer after another.
item.content:encoded: The system updates your phone receives include security fixes, and Apple's support pages for Taiwan and mainland China list keeping software up to date as one of the most important steps you can take to keep an Apple device secure. According to an analysis written afterwards by MIT researchers, from 2 November 1988 a program broke into computers on the internet, which then had about 60,000 hosts, and spread from one machine to the next. It exploited a debugging feature that the mail-handling program left on by default and a service for looking up user information that did not check the length of its input, and it guessed passwords from account names, simple variations of people's names and a word list built into the program. In the paper's account of the defences used at the time, removing the mail program's debug command and shutting down or fixing the lookup service each worked only once the other holes had been plugged as well. On an iPhone, turn on automatic installation under Settings > General > Software Update > Automatic Updates; Google's Android help page in Chinese said as of 1 November that most system updates and security patches install automatically, though timing varies by device, manufacturer and carrier, and older devices may not be able to run newer versions.

item.title: The switch for personalised recommendations in apps
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: If you have used the mainland Chinese version of an app, its settings may include an option to turn off personalised recommendations. On this day, China's Personal Information Protection Law took effect, requiring businesses that push information through automated decision-making to offer an option not based on personal characteristics or an easy way to refuse.
item.content:encoded: In an assessment published in March 2023 by Shanghai's municipal consumer rights protection commission (republished by Sina Finance), all 10 commonly used apps tested had a way to turn off personalised recommendations (content picked from what you browse and tap), and only Xiaohongshu (RedNote) said that turning them off would not stop them entirely. China's Personal Information Protection Law took effect on 1 November 2021 and requires businesses that push information or marketing through automated decision-making (choosing content by a person's characteristics) to also offer an option not based on those characteristics or an easy way to refuse, and under the 2022 algorithmic recommendation provisions a provider must stop the related service immediately once a user switches recommendations off. State bodies handling personal information must also notify the people concerned under the 2021 law, unless other laws require confidentiality or notice would hinder the body in performing its statutory duties. The Personal Data Protection Act of Taiwan does not mention advertising or recommendations, and its Article 20 covers only marketing, with no requirement for a recommendation switch or an option not based on personal characteristics. Article 20(2) and (3) do require a business that uses personal data for marketing under that article to stop once you refuse and to offer a way to refuse the first time it markets to you, so readers in Taiwan can turn down marketing that uses their personal data (checked in October 2026).

item.title: The identity details you register for a phone number
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: If you get a mobile phone number in Taiwan or Japan, the carrier has to check who you are when you sign up. On this day, Indonesia began requiring people signing up for prepaid SIM cards to verify their national ID number and family card number against the government's population database.
item.content:encoded: Carriers in Taiwan must check and record a subscriber's name, address and two identity document numbers before activating any line, prepaid or not, and carriers in Japan must confirm a subscriber's name, address and date of birth when signing a contract for mobile voice service. On 31 October 2017, Indonesia's communications ministry began requiring people signing up for prepaid SIM cards to verify their national ID number and family card (household registration) number against the population registry's database, which Bisnis.com reported the ministry as saying was meant to prevent misuse of phone numbers. In March 2018, detikInet reported that one ID number had been used to register 50 phone numbers, which the ministry's written statement called unauthorised use rather than a data leak, and that ID and family card numbers were also circulating on websites. ANTARA and Bisnis.com reported the current communications and digital ministry as saying that Indonesian citizens have had to register new numbers with their ID number plus facial recognition since July 2026, and that each identity may hold at most three prepaid numbers per carrier (checked in October 2026). Readers outside Indonesia do not need to do anything because of these rules.

item.title: Web addresses starting with xn-- in the address bar
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Your browser switches to a code starting with xn-- in the address bar when a Chinese, Korean or other non-Latin domain name looks like a possible imitation of another site. On this day, the ICANN Board approved a fast-track process that let countries and territories apply to write the last part of a web address in their own script.
item.content:encoded: Browsers convert the Chinese, Korean or other non-Latin characters in a domain name into a string of plain letters and digits starting with xn-- before looking up the site's address. When the name matches a pattern that Chrome or Firefox treats as a possible lookalike, such as Latin letters mixed with Cyrillic or Greek, the address bar shows that code instead (Chrome's rules do allow Latin letters mixed with Chinese, Japanese or Korean). At its meeting in Seoul on 30 October 2009, ICANN (the body that oversees the world's domain names) approved a fast-track process for countries and territories to apply for the last part of a web address, where .tw or .kr sits, in their own script. In the list of top-level domains kept by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), .中国 and .中國 were delegated on 8 July 2010, .香港 on 12 July, .台灣 on 14 July and .ไทย on 17 August, with .한국 and .新加坡 following on 6 February 2011. Readers can open the sites they use often from a bookmark or by typing the address, and because Chrome's documentation says password managers fill in a password only when the domain matches exactly, a saved password that fails to appear is a cue to check the address (both suggestions are our inference, and the sources do not assess how well they work).

item.title: End-to-end encryption and spyware on the device
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The end-to-end encryption on your phone protects messages in transit but cannot stop the phone itself from being compromised. On this day, WhatsApp and Facebook sued the spyware company NSO Group in a US federal court, alleging that it had used WhatsApp to send spyware to about 1,400 phones and devices.
item.content:encoded: End-to-end encryption keeps a message unreadable in transit, even to the servers that carry it, but a message on a compromised phone can still be read once it has been decrypted there. On 29 October 2019, WhatsApp and Facebook (now Meta) sued the spyware company NSO Group in the US District Court for the Northern District of California; according to the complaint, the defendants could not break WhatsApp's end-to-end encryption, so they used WhatsApp's servers to send malware to about 1,400 phones and devices and read messages after decryption. In November 2025 the court entered judgment and a permanent injunction barring NSO from targeting WhatsApp with spyware; NSO asked for the injunction to be put on hold, arguing that it would cause irreparable harm to its business, and the appeals court denied the request in January 2026. Anyone can keep their apps and phone software up to date, a general rule we draw from WhatsApp asking users to update the app after it patched the vulnerability used in the attack. People who need to protect their sources can consider Lockdown Mode on an iPhone (its help page lists no regional limits), which according to Apple's support page is designed to reduce the attack surface that mercenary spyware could potentially exploit, at the cost of blocking most message attachments and link previews (only general protections are listed on the help page for Android's Advanced Protection).

item.title: Face data registered for building access and venue entry
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Face data you register for building access or member entry can identify you just as a fingerprint can. On this day, a university associate professor in mainland China sued a Hangzhou zoo that had switched its annual-pass entry from fingerprints to facial recognition.
item.content:encoded: Face data you register for building access or member entry can identify you just as a fingerprint can. On 28 October 2019, a university associate professor in mainland China filed a lawsuit with the Fuyang District People's Court in Hangzhou against a zoo, because the zoo had switched entry for annual-pass holders from fingerprints, which the professor had registered, to facial recognition. In 2020 the first-instance court found that checking visitors by fingerprint or facial recognition was lawful in itself, but because the two sides had agreed on fingerprint entry and the zoo had not told the plaintiff what the photos were for, the court ordered the zoo to delete the plaintiff's facial data, and in 2021 the appeal court upheld the ruling and also ordered the zoo to delete the plaintiff's fingerprint data, since the zoo had stopped using its fingerprint gates. In Japan, according to a report in the Akita Sakigake Shimpo in October 2025, JR East had in July stopped using face-recognition security cameras at some Tokyo-area stations (meant to detect wanted suspects and alert the police); the Japan Federation of Bar Associations had asked it to stop using them over privacy concerns, and JR East gave its reason as the end of a contract with an outside company and a review of the cameras' effectiveness. Wherever you are, when you are asked to register your face you can first ask whether a card or QR code would work instead.

item.title: Personal information in search results and removal requests
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: You can ask Google to stop listing pages that contain your phone number, home address or ID number in its search results. On this day, Indonesia's House of Representatives passed amendments to the Electronic Information and Transactions Law, requiring website and platform operators to delete irrelevant information at a person's request on the basis of a court ruling.
item.content:encoded: You can ask Google to stop listing pages that contain your phone number, home address or ID number in its search results, though removing the page itself means contacting the site owner. On 27 October 2016, Indonesia's House of Representatives passed amendments to the Electronic Information and Transactions (ITE) Law, under which website and platform operators must delete irrelevant information at the request of the person concerned, on the basis of a court ruling. The Jakarta Post quoted the information and telecommunications minister as calling this good because Indonesia previously had no right to be forgotten, and the paper reported that this provision and the articles on cyberbullying were regarded as particularly draconian. The lawmaker who led the House team on the amendments highlighted Article 40, which authorizes the government to cut off access to unlawful content or order providers to do so, saying the aim is to make the government responsible for preventing the spread of prohibited information, while the paper reported that the law has little in the way of provisions regulating the use of this power. That power remains in the second amendment, Law No. 1 of 2024, which adds that for pornography, gambling and other content defined by regulation such an order can take the form of cutting off access or having the provider moderate the content itself, as far as technically possible; if you would rather not deal with a site owner, you can start by asking Google to remove only the search result.

item.title: Websites that fail to load and domain name blocking
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: When a website will not load for you, one possible reason is that your internet provider has made its address impossible to look up. On this day, the chair of the US House Judiciary Committee introduced the Stop Online Piracy Act, under which internet providers acting on a court order were to take measures such as stopping the domain names of foreign infringing sites from resolving.
item.content:encoded: When a website will not load for you, one possible reason is that your internet provider has stopped the internet's phone book (DNS) from returning the address of the server behind it. On 26 October 2011, the chair of the US House Judiciary Committee introduced the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA), under which an internet provider served with a court order was to take measures within 5 days, or within a period set by the court, including stopping the domain name of a foreign infringing site from resolving. In January 2012 the chair announced plans to remove the DNS blocking provision, Wikipedia went dark for 24 hours in protest, and the committee later put off action on the bill. In Asia, Singapore's Copyright Act 2021 lets the High Court order a network connection provider to take reasonable steps to disable access to a flagrantly infringing online location, while according to a Japanese government anti-piracy plan, reissued in August 2026, legislation on blocking will be considered in light of how other measures work and the extent of the damage, and we found no provision in Taiwan's Copyright Act, as amended in June 2022, that lets rights holders seek site blocking (we did not look into blocking on other grounds). If a site will not load on your network, the Web Connectivity test in OONI Probe, the app from OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference), can separate DNS, connection and page-content anomalies, though an anomaly does not always mean blocking, and according to OONI's FAQ, running the app can potentially be risky depending on your threat model and the country.

item.title: Third-party apps you signed in to with Facebook
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Apps or games you once signed in to with your Facebook account may still hold data they took from it at the time. On this day, the UK's Information Commissioner's Office announced a £500,000 fine on Facebook, citing among other reasons that it let app developers obtain users' data without sufficiently clear and informed consent.
item.content:encoded: Apps or games you once signed in to with your Facebook account may still hold data they took from it at the time. On 25 October 2018, the UK's Information Commissioner's Office (ICO, the regulator responsible for data protection) announced a £500,000 fine on Facebook, and its press release states that between 2007 and 2014 Facebook let app developers obtain users' data without sufficiently clear and informed consent, including the data of people who had not installed an app but were friends of someone who had. Facebook appealed and agreed in the 2019 settlement to pay the fine without admitting liability, saying, in the ICO's 2019 statement on the settlement, that it should have done more in 2015 to investigate claims about the political consultancy Cambridge Analytica and had by then significantly restricted the information app developers could access. In April 2018, Facebook put the maximum at 87 million people, mostly in the US, whose information may have been improperly shared with Cambridge Analytica, and its chart of the ten countries with the most people whose information may have been shared includes the Philippines (1,175,870), Indonesia (1,096,666), India (562,455) and Vietnam (427,446), while Marketing-Interactive reported a figure from Facebook of potentially 65,009 for Singapore. Facebook's Help Center (checked in October 2026) shows that on a computer you can remove an app under Settings & privacy > Settings > Apps and websites, though the app may still have information it stored earlier.
